justification_text:
The point estimates I made at each horizon (1 day, 1 week, and 1 month) were based on the trends, patterns, and dynamics of the underlying system or market I was forecasting. At the shortest horizon (1 day), my estimate of 79.93 reflects a very high reliance on the most recent data, assuming a degree of short-term stability. Small changes in the system are unlikely to have accumulated significantly over just a single day. Over one week, the point estimate shifts slightly to 80.1, accounting for the possibility of small drift or momentum in the data, as well as allowing time for minor adjustments to play out. By the one-month horizon, the estimate grows further to 80.5, reflecting the influence of longer-term systemic pressures and gradual trends that could act on the underlying variable.

The width of the confidence intervals reflects the uncertainty inherent at each time horizon. For 1 day, the interval is relatively narrow, spanning just 0.28 on either side of the point estimate. This tight range is because it’s easier to predict short-term behavior with confidence; there’s simply less time for unexpected events to cause disruptions. By 1 week, the 90% confidence interval widens considerably to span 2.42, reflecting the complexity and unpredictability that comes with a longer timescale. Over a month, the confidence interval continues to widen to 5.3, as more variables, events, and potential shocks could potentially influence the system. Essentially, uncertainty grows over time as there’s more opportunity for random or unforeseen factors to come into play.

Even with these confidence intervals, there are always risks that could push outcomes outside the stated ranges. These might include major shocks, such as geopolitical events, unexpected economic developments, or abrupt shifts in market psychology, any of which could drive short-term volatility well beyond my expectations. Additionally, structural breaks—situations where the underlying system undergoes a significant change—could invalidate the assumptions behind my forecast. If, for instance, an event occurs that fundamentally alters a key variable (e.g., a policy change or major disaster), the actual outcome might fall outside my confidence intervals. Forecasting always carries this element of risk, as no model can account for every possible source of uncertainty.
